普圖圖海螺號是以東太平洋大型海螺殼製成的氣鳴樂器。製作時切去螺塔尖端並磨孔，形成: The pututu conch horn is an aerophone made from the large shell of an eastern Pacific conch. To make it, the tip of the spire is cut away and a hole ground out to form a mouthpiece, producing a wind instrument rather like a trumpet. Its raw material is the shell of the true conch and its close relatives. The Chavín culture of the Andean highlands of northern Peru used conch horns of this kind; in the Andean region this playable shell is still called the pututu and used for music.
普圖圖海螺號的發聲體為東太平洋大型海螺殼，屬氣鳴樂器，來源支持其用於安地斯地區。: The sounding body of the pututu is the large shell of an eastern Pacific conch; it is an aerophone, and the source supports its use in the Andean region. The shell is thick and heavy, ivory white to light brown outside with a bright white opening; to make the instrument the tip of the spire is cut away and a hole ground out as a mouthpiece, and no other part's material is mentioned.
普圖圖海螺號起源於南美洲安地斯山脈地區，其歷史可追溯至古老的查溫文明時期。查溫文: The pututu conch horn originated in the Andean mountain region of South America, and its history goes back to the time of the ancient Chavín culture. The Chavín culture is an important early civilisation of the Andean highlands of northern Peru, and its people were the first to find and use the shells of the California giant conch to make wind instruments. The California giant conch is distributed along the eastern Pacific coast, from the Gulf of California down to Peru, and its huge shell provided an ideal material for instruments. Over time, the technique of making and using this instrument was passed down from generation to generation in the Andean region and became an important part of the local traditional music culture. To this day the people of Peru and the surrounding Andean region keep the tradition of the pututu, using it in religious ritual, folk music performance and cultural celebration, a witness to the long and enduring life of this ancient instrument.
普圖圖海螺號音色渾厚而富有穿透力，帶有明顯的低頻共鳴與溫暖的質感。其音域偏低，音: The pututu has a thick, penetrating timbre, with a clear low-frequency resonance and a warm quality. Its range is low, and the pitch depends on the size of the shell and on the playing technique; it usually produces a deep, solemn tone. The instrument relies on the cavity of the natural shell for its resonance, which gives a bleak quality with the feel of the sea. Beside the sharp brightness of brass instruments, the conch horn sounds more archaic and heavy; and unlike the clear sound of a bamboo flute, its timbre is more primal and more ritual. The sound travels a long way, and when it is used in the Andes for religious ritual and for gathering signals it has a striking power to move. The instrument preserves the musical residue of the ancient Chavín civilisation, and its sound is distinctive and culturally rich.
